Estimate Memory Requirements for Multiscale Optimization

Source: R/estimate_multiscale_ram.R
estimate_multiscale_ram.Rd

Estimates how much memory a kernel_prep() object (and optionally a fitted starting model) needs during multiScale_optim(), and recommends a conservative maximum number of parallel workers (n_cores). Use it before running a large or slow model in parallel, because each worker holds its own copy of the inputs.

Usage

estimate_multiscale_ram(
  kernel_inputs,
  fitted_mod = NULL,
  join_by = NULL,
  refit_fn = NULL,
  n_cores = NULL,
  PSOCK = (.Platform$OS.type != "unix"),
  safety_factor = 1.5,
  ram_fraction = 0.75,
  leave_free = 2L
)

# S3 method for class 'multiScaleR_ram'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

kernel_inputs

A multiScaleR_data object created by kernel_prep() or kernel_prep_by_group().

fitted_mod

Optional fitted starting model, as you would pass to multiScale_optim(). When supplied, the estimate also includes the optimization context sent to each worker. Without it, the estimate can understate the real payload. Default: NULL.

join_by

Optional data frame passed through to multiScale_optim() for unmarked workflows. Default: NULL.

refit_fn

Optional custom refit function passed through to multiScale_optim(). Default: NULL.

n_cores

Optional positive integer. Worker count at which to report the peak memory estimate. When omitted, the recommended maximum is used.

PSOCK

Logical. Budget workers as PSOCK (socket) workers. Default: TRUE on Windows and FALSE on Unix-like systems. The estimate is the same either way, because forked workers are also budgeted as though each holds its own copy.

safety_factor

Numeric scalar, at least 1. Multiplier on each worker's payload to allow for temporary allocations during optimization. Larger values give fewer recommended workers. Default: 1.5.

ram_fraction

Numeric scalar between 0 and 1. Share of total system RAM treated as usable. The rest is left for the operating system and other R objects. Default: 0.75.

leave_free

Non-negative integer. Number of physical CPU cores to leave unused when computing the CPU limit. Default: 2.

x

A multiScaleR_ram object returned by estimate_multiscale_ram().

...

Not used.

Value

estimate_multiscale_ram() returns a list of class multiScaleR_ram with these elements:

  • requested_n_cores: the worker count used for the peak estimate (n_cores, or the recommendation when n_cores is omitted).

  • recommended_n_cores: the smaller of the CPU and RAM limits, or the CPU limit when RAM could not be detected. Never less than 1.

  • max_cores_by_cpu: physical cores minus leave_free, at least 1.

  • max_cores_by_ram: the number of workers that fit in the usable RAM, at least 1, or NA when total RAM could not be detected.

  • backend: "PSOCK" or "fork", the assumed parallel backend.

  • system: list with the detected physical_cores and logical_cores, leave_free, total_ram_bytes, usable_ram_fraction, usable_ram_bytes, safety_factor, and readable versions of the RAM values (total_ram_pretty, usable_ram_pretty).

  • point_summary: one-row data frame with the number of points, the mean, median, and maximum number of extracted cells per point (NA in lean mode), the number of source layers, whether cell-level data are stored (cell_data_stored), and the number of distance bins (nbins).

  • component_bytes: data frame with columns component, bytes, and pretty (a readable size) for each stored object (kernel_inputs_total, kernel_dat, d_list, raw_cov, binned, join_by, fitted_mod, opt_context), the two bundles described in Details (worker_bundle and main_bundle), and peak_parallel_estimate.

  • notes: character vector of interpretation notes and detection warnings.

print() displays the main limits, the detected hardware, the peak estimate, and the notes, and returns x invisibly.

How the estimate is built

Sizes come from utils::object.size(), so they describe stored R objects, not the transient memory used by exactextractr, model refits, or linear algebra libraries. The main bundle is what the main R session holds (the kernel inputs, join_by, the optimization context, and the model). The worker bundle is what each parallel worker receives (the per-cell distances and values, join_by, the optimization context, and the model). The limits and the peak estimate follow from these sizes.

  • Usable RAM = total RAM x ram_fraction.

  • RAM limit = (usable RAM - main bundle) / (worker bundle x safety_factor), rounded down.

  • Peak estimate = main bundle + n_cores x worker bundle x safety_factor.

Even where forking lets workers share memory, each worker is budgeted as if it held its own copy. Hardware measurements that succeed are kept for the rest of the R session. A failed RAM lookup is retried on the next call.

Read the report

Compare the worker count you plan to use with max_cores_by_ram, and read the peak estimate at that count. These are conservative estimates, not measured memory use. The recommendation is never below one worker, but that does not guarantee a serial run fits in memory. A run at or below the limit can still run out of memory during a model refit. If RAM detection or the estimate fails, no limit can be enforced.

Reduce the memory needed

When every covariate is a kernel mean, rebuild the original kernel_prep() call with bin = TRUE, store_cell_data = FALSE, keeping its other settings, and check the estimate again. This lean mode keeps only the distance-binned summaries that optimization uses. It is not available for landscape or surface metrics, which need the cell-level data. Otherwise, use fewer workers or n_cores = 1. Do not delete components of the object by hand, and do not shrink a scientifically chosen max_D only to pass the check.

How multiScale_optim() uses the estimate

With n_cores > 1, multiScale_optim() calls this function with its default settings before starting workers. It stops with an error when n_cores exceeds max_cores_by_ram. It does not lower n_cores for you. When RAM cannot be detected or the estimate fails, the check does not block the run.

See also

multiScale_optim(), kernel_prep(). The section "Estimate the scales of effect" in vignette("v02-user-guide", package = "multiScaleR") shows the check on a worked example.

Examples

data("pts")
data("count_data")
hab <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "hab.tif",
                               package = "multiScaleR"))
kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts, raster_stack = hab, max_D = 250,
                             kernel = "gaussian", verbose = FALSE)
mod <- glm(y ~ hab, family = poisson,
           data = data.frame(count_data["y"], kernel_inputs$kernel_dat))

# Recommended worker limits and the peak memory estimate for two workers
ram <- estimate_multiscale_ram(kernel_inputs, fitted_mod = mod, n_cores = 2)
ram
#> 
#> Estimated parallel RAM budget for `multiScaleR`
#> Backend assumption: fork
#> Recommended max workers: 2
#> CPU limit after reserve: 2
#> RAM limit: 2975
#> Physical cores detected: 4
#> Logical cores detected: 4
#> Total RAM detected: 15.6 Gb
#> Usable RAM budget: 11.7 Gb
#> Peak estimate at 2 worker(s): 11.1 Mb
#> 
#> Notes:
#> - Parallel RAM budgeting remains conservative even when forked workers may share memory.

# Estimated size of each component, largest first
ram$component_bytes[order(-ram$component_bytes$bytes), ]
